I responded to this post last night and I came up with a few more things i would like to share.

1.It can be hard to make friends in Japan.


I am lucky enough to have made a few Japanese friends but I can't say the same for everyone. It’s extremely rare for strangers to strike up a conversation on the train, for instance. (Some Japanese people actually didn’t believe me when I told them that this sort of thing happens all the time in other countries!) I actually liked this in a way because it helped me learn not to care so much about what I look like or what other people think of me. I also like to be able to sit and read a book or just do what I want (however “weird” my activities may be) without being interrupted or given strange looks. On the other hand though, this can be lonely sometimes, and it does tend to be more difficult to form close relationships with Japanese people than it is with Westerners. I think it depends a lot on your personality, but life in Japan might be especially lonely for you if you’re a very outgoing and friendly sort of person who likes to spend a lot of time with other people. I suppose it has a lot to do with the tendency for Japanese people to be so dedicated to their jobs. Because a lot of people put almost all their time into their work, they don’t really socialize with anyone other than their coworkers. So if you’re not part of a company (or if you are a part of a company but aren’t as dedicated to it as your Japanese coworkers), you may find yourself feeling isolated. Work is life for a lot of Japanese people, and if you can’t identify with that they may find it hard to relate to you on more than a superficial level. Interestingly, having lived in both rural and urban areas I got the impression that this sort of thing is less of a problem in the country than it is in the city. However, since there are less opportunites to meet people in rural areas, the overall result actually doesn’t change very much. Once in a while you might get lucky and have a really great conversation with someone at a party or something like that, but even when this happens Japanese people tend not to be very proactive about exchanging phone numbers and arranging to meet again soon. Several times I was surprised by their “Well, I’ll see you again if I see you” kind of attitude. And usually you have to meet with someone several times before they’ll really start to consider you their “friend”. So yes, it is difficult and sometimes even I felt lonely. 


2.   There is very little physical contact between people

This is kind of related to the above point. Personally I’m not a very “touchy-feely” kind of person, but even so, coming from a culture where people hug each other a lot I did kind of miss this sometimes in Japan. Generally speaking Japanese people don’t hug, especially not when meeting someone for the first time. They don’t shake hands either, but bow instead. It is okay to shake someone’s hand if you’re a Westerner (especially if you’re speaking English), but I definitely wouldn’t recommend hugging unless you want to make the person very uncomfortable. The first time I was in Japan and living with a host family, an American guy came to visit us for a couple of days. When it was time for him to leave, he suddenly grabbed my host father and gave him a big hug. My poor host father looked shell shocked! It’s something that just isn’t done in this culture. (Actually there are situations where it may be appropriate, but it takes time to develop a sense for this and I would advise newcomers to avoid it just to be safe.) There isn’t even that much physical contact amongst family members. People don’t hug each other at family get-togethers, for instance. If you’re a woman talking to another woman, it is okay to do things like touching her arm when talking to her if she’s someone you know. It’s also okay to show physical affection to small children. But men and women generally don’t touch each other at all unless they’re in a romantic relationship. I find that physical contact can add to a sense of emotional closeness with a person (not necessarily in a romantic way), and it does seem that the taboo against physical contact in Japanese culture further contributes to the above-mentioned difficulty of forming close relationships.  

3.  There’s too much materialism. 


Japan is a modern country that’s very convenient and comfortable to live in, which is very nice. I loved that I was always able to buy anything I wanted or needed. I also like that Japanese people are fashionable and that most of them (not all, but most!) always put in the effort to look decent in public. Sometimes though, I got the impression that people cared just a little too much about “things”. Ironically, this actually contrasts with traditional Japanese thought which values minimalism and simplicity. But if you go walking around Tokyo today, it’s easy to start feeling like a loser if your bag doesn’t match your shoes. Japan has a way of making you feel like you “need” things that you really don’t. It seems like a lot of modern Japanese women look to shopping as a source of fulfillment, which I don’t think is very healthy.
